Merge and Customise Tables

Source: vignettes/merge-tables.Rmd
merge-tables.Rmd

A manuscript table often brings several analyses together: the baseline characteristics, the crude estimates and the adjusted estimates, or a primary analysis next to its sensitivity analyses. merge_tables() places any number of gtregression tables side by side, aligns the rows by variable and category, and keeps every footnote.

This article covers:

  • merging two, three or more tables;
  • labelling each block with spanners;
  • keeping binary rows consistent;
  • merging sensitivity analyses and survival models;
  • relabelling the merged table with modify_table();
  • further styling with flextable functions;
  • saving the result.

Example data 

library(gtregression)
library(dplyr)

data("data_birthwt", package = "gtregression")

birthwt <- data_birthwt |>
  mutate(
    race = factor(race, levels = c(1, 2, 3), labels = c("White", "Black", "Other")),
    smoke = factor(smoke, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    ht = factor(ht, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    ui = factor(ui, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    low = factor(low, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Normal BW", "Low BW"))
  )

attr(birthwt$age, "label") <- "Maternal age (years)"
attr(birthwt$lwt, "label") <- "Maternal weight (lb)"
attr(birthwt$race, "label") <- "Race"
attr(birthwt$smoke, "label") <- "Smoking during pregnancy"
attr(birthwt$ht, "label") <- "History of hypertension"
attr(birthwt$ui, "label") <- "Uterine irritability"

exposures <- c("age", "lwt", "race", "smoke", "ht", "ui")

Build the tables you want to combine

Use the same binary layout in every table you plan to merge. Showing both levels in the descriptive table and the reference row in each regression table gives one row per category across the whole merged table.

desc <- descriptive_table(
  birthwt,
  exposures = exposures,
  by = "low",
  show_dichotomous = "all_levels"
)

crude <- uni_reg(
  birthwt,
  outcome = "low",
  exposures = exposures,
  approach = "logit",
  show_ref = TRUE
)

adjusted <- multi_reg(
  birthwt,
  outcome = "low",
  exposures = exposures,
  approach = "logit",
  show_ref = TRUE
)

Merge two tables

Supply the tables in the order they should appear, and one spanner label per table.

crude_adjusted <- merge_tables(
  crude,
  adjusted,
  spanners = c("Crude", "Adjusted")
)

Merge three or more tables

There is no limit of two: pass as many tables as you need. The classic “Table 2” combines the descriptive summary, the crude estimates and the adjusted estimates.

table_2 <- merge_tables(
  desc,
  crude,
  adjusted,
  spanners = c("Low birth weight", "Crude", "Adjusted")
)

Rows are matched on the underlying variable and category, not on the visible label, so the tables stay aligned even when labels differ. A variable that appears in some tables but not in others is kept and left blank where it was not analysed.

If one table shows binary variables as a single row and another shows both levels, merge_tables() warns and names the settings that make them compatible (show_dichotomous = "all_levels" with show_ref = TRUE, or show_dichotomous = "single_row" with show_ref = FALSE, used consistently).

Sensitivity analyses side by side

Tables of the same type can be merged too. Here a primary model is shown next to a model restricted to mothers without hypertension and a model with fewer covariates.

primary <- multi_reg(
  birthwt,
  outcome = "low",
  exposures = c("smoke", "race", "ui"),
  adjust_for = c("age", "lwt"),
  approach = "logit",
  show_ref = TRUE
)

no_hypertension <- multi_reg(
  filter(birthwt, ht == "No"),
  outcome = "low",
  exposures = c("smoke", "race", "ui"),
  adjust_for = c("age", "lwt"),
  approach = "logit",
  show_ref = TRUE
)

fewer_covariates <- multi_reg(
  birthwt,
  outcome = "low",
  exposures = c("smoke", "race", "ui"),
  adjust_for = "age",
  approach = "logit",
  show_ref = TRUE
)

sensitivity <- merge_tables(
  primary,
  no_hypertension,
  fewer_covariates,
  spanners = c("Primary analysis", "Without hypertension", "Age-adjusted only")
)

Each adjustment note is carried over from its own table, so readers can see exactly what each block was adjusted for.

Survival tables

Cox and parametric survival tables merge in the same way. Unadjusted and adjusted hazard ratios are a common pair.

data("data_lungcancer", package = "gtregression")

lung <- data_lungcancer |>
  mutate(
    trt = factor(trt, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Standard", "Test")),
    celltype = factor(celltype)
  )

cox_crude <- cox_reg(
  lung,
  time = "time",
  event = "status",
  exposures = c("trt", "celltype", "karno"),
  show_ref = TRUE
)

cox_adjusted <- cox_reg(
  lung,
  time = "time",
  event = "status",
  exposures = c("trt", "celltype", "karno"),
  multivariable = TRUE,
  show_ref = TRUE
)

survival_table <- merge_tables(
  cox_crude,
  cox_adjusted,
  spanners = c("Unadjusted HR", "Adjusted HR")
)

Relabel with modify_table()

modify_table() works on merged tables. Use the original variable names on the left-hand side; the visible labels can be anything.

table_2_final <- modify_table(
  table_2,
  variable_labels = c(lwt = "Weight at last menstrual period (lb)"),
  level_labels = list(smoke = c(Yes = "Smoker", No = "Non-smoker")),
  caption = "Table 2. Factors associated with low birth weight",
  caveat = "Odds ratios from logistic regression; adjusted estimates include all listed characteristics."
)

Choose a table theme

Every table function and merge_tables() accept a theme. Presets are "minimal" (the default), "clinical", "striped", "shaded" and "jama". You can also combine primitives: "plain", "zebra", "lines", "labels_bold", "compact" and "header_shaded".

jama_table <- merge_tables(
  crude,
  adjusted,
  spanners = c("Crude", "Adjusted"),
  theme = "jama"
)

Fine-tune with flextable

The merged table is an ordinary flextable stored in $table. Anything the flextable package can do can be applied to it: fonts, colours, widths, alignment or highlighting particular cells. Take the table out, change it, and keep the result.

library(flextable)

ft <- table_2_final$table

ft <- ft |>
  font(fontname = "Arial", part = "all") |>
  fontsize(size = 9, part = "all") |>
  color(color = "#0F5C5F", part = "header") |>
  bg(bg = "#EEF6F6", part = "header") |>
  align(j = 2:ncol_keys(ft), align = "center", part = "all") |>
  autofit()

ft

To change particular cells, refer to columns by their keys and to rows by number or by a condition on the cell values. Each block of a merged table has its own keys, ending in _p1, _p2, _p3 and so on, in the order the tables were merged.

ft$col_keys
#> [1] "Characteristic"          "Normal.BW_p1"           
#> [3] "Low.BW_p1"               "N_p2"                   
#> [5] "OR..95..CI._p2"          "p.value_p2"             
#> [7] "N_p3"                    "Adjusted.OR..95..CI._p3"
#> [9] "p.value_p3"

For example, to bold the adjusted p-values below 0.05 (the third block):

adjusted_p <- ft$col_keys[startsWith(ft$col_keys, "p.value") & endsWith(ft$col_keys, "_p3")]
p_values <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(sub("<", "", ft$body$dataset[[adjusted_p]])))

ft <- bold(ft, i = which(p_values < 0.05), j = adjusted_p, part = "body")
ft

Changes made this way apply to the flextable only. Keep the original gtregression object if you want to merge it again later, and apply flextable styling as the final step.

For HTML-first work, use format = "gt" in merge_tables() and style the result with the gt package in the same way.

Save the result

save_table() accepts the gtregression object or a styled flextable. The file type is set by format.

save_table(table_2_final, filename = "table-2", format = "docx")
save_table(ft, filename = "table-2-styled", format = "docx")
save_table(table_2_final, filename = "table-2", format = "html")

Several tables can go into one Word document with save_docx():

save_docx(
  tables = list(table_2_final, primary),
  filename = "results",
  titles = c("Table 2. Low birth weight", "Table 3. Sensitivity analyses")
)

Which tables can be merged?

Can be merged Notes
descriptive_table() Use show_dichotomous consistently.
uni_reg(), multi_reg() and the stratified functions Use show_ref consistently.
cox_reg(), surv_reg(), competing_risk_reg() Crude and adjusted pairs, or sensitivity analyses.
ordinal_reg(), multinomial_reg(), multilevel_reg(), conditional_logit_reg() Each keeps its own estimate type and notes.
A merged table Merge again, or relabel with modify_table().

risk_difference() tables are designed to stand alone and are not merged; see Risk Difference and NNT.
